reconciled_candidates.label: Real options definition and contrast with DCF/NPV
reconciled_candidates.description: Real options extend financial options theory to business investments, capturing the value of flexibility and learning under uncertainty that traditional DCF/NPV undervalues. They enable delayed, expanded, or abandoned decisions, turning negative expected value into positive by staging investments.
coverage_criteria: Define real options and contrast them with static investment analysis like NPV.
Explain why traditional DCF can undervalue assets with embedded flexibility.
Identify at least two types of real options (delay, expand, abandon).
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: These candidates all define real options and explain why they address the limitations of NPV/DCF. Together they form a complete introductory concept.

reconciled_candidates.label: Learning and adaptive behavior in real options
reconciled_candidates.description: Real option value stems from the ability to observe outcomes (learn) and adjust actions (adaptive behavior). Staging investments transforms a negative NPV into positive by acting on new information. This shifts management focus from avoiding uncertainty to maximizing learning and flexibility.
coverage_criteria: Restate why a two-step investment can outperform a one-step investment with the same overall probabilities.
Describe the mindset shift from static NPV planning to proactive real options thinking.
List the four strategic improvements from real options thinking (emphasize opportunities, enhance leverage, maximize rights, minimize obligations).
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: One candidate details the mechanical value creation through staged investment, while the other describes the resulting managerial mindset. Combined, they capture both the intuition and strategic adoption.

reconciled_candidates.label: Using payoff diagrams to identify real options
reconciled_candidates.description: A real option exists when the payoff structure resembles a call or put option diagram, featuring a kinked payoff limiting downside losses while allowing upside gains. This visual criterion helps recognize embedded options in business decisions.

reconciled_candidates.label: Three definitional characteristics of a real option
reconciled_candidates.description: To qualify as a real option, an asset or decision must have: (1) a clearly defined underlying asset whose value varies unpredictably, (2) contingent payoffs triggered by a specific event, and (3) a limited life.
coverage_criteria: List the three characteristics.
For a given business scenario, determine whether these characteristics are present.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: This candidate presents a precise checklist; it is best kept as a standalone concept for clear recall and application.

reconciled_candidates.label: Exclusivity as driver of significant option value
reconciled_candidates.description: An option has significant economic value only if the holder has exclusivity—the sole right to exercise it. Without exclusivity (e.g., anyone can buy at market price), the option value is zero.
coverage_criteria: Explain why exclusivity is necessary for a real option to have economic value.
Contrast the landlord anecdote scenario with a proprietary technology option.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: This candidate focuses on a crucial filter with a memorable anecdote; it merits its own concept due to its decision-making importance.

reconciled_candidates.label: Six determinants of real option value
reconciled_candidates.description: The value of a real option is driven by six factors: underlying asset value, variance of that value, expected dividends, strike price, option life, and risk-free interest rate. Uncertainty (variance) uniquely increases option value because of asymmetric payoffs, contrary to NPV logic.
coverage_criteria: List the six determinants and their real-market equivalents.
Explain why higher variance increases option value, while higher dividends reduce it.
Predict the directional effect of a change in each determinant on a call option.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: All three candidates describe the same lever framework; merging them ensures a complete explanation of each determinant and its effect.

reconciled_candidates.label: Replication and arbitrage principles in option pricing
reconciled_candidates.description: Option pricing models rely on: (1) replication—constructing a portfolio of the underlying asset and borrowing/lending that mimics the option's payoffs; (2) arbitrage—if two assets have identical payoffs, they must have the same price.
coverage_criteria: Describe what a replicating portfolio is.
Explain why arbitrage forces options and replicating portfolios to have equal prices.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: This candidate explains the foundational principles behind valuation models; it stands alone as a theoretical prerequisite.

reconciled_candidates.label: Model choice: Black-Scholes vs. binomial for real options
reconciled_candidates.description: The Black-Scholes model assumes European exercise, constant variance, and no jumps, requiring only six inputs. The binomial model allows early exercise and changing variances but demands detailed price path data, often infeasible for real assets. Practitioners often prefer Black-Scholes for its parsimony.
coverage_criteria: State the key restrictive assumptions of Black-Scholes.
Contrast the data requirements of the binomial model with its flexibility.
Articulate why practitioners might still prefer Black-Scholes despite its limitations.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: A single candidate covers the practical model trade-offs; it is a decision-oriented concept best kept intact.

reconciled_candidates.label: Proactive vs. reactive flexibility in real options
reconciled_candidates.description: Reactive flexibility involves optimally exercising an existing option; proactive flexibility means managers can influence option value levers (e.g., increase uncertainty, extend duration) before exercise. Unlike financial options in deep markets, real options exist in contexts with few players, enabling proactive influence.
coverage_criteria: Distinguish between reactive and proactive flexibility and give an example of each.
Explain why the limited-player environment in real business situations enables proactive flexibility.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: One defines the two types, the other explains the enabling context; together they form a complete strategic lesson.
